newsitem.title: ITALY: BOXING-ITALIAN STRIPPED OF GOLD IN SCORING ROW.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-ITALIAN STRIPPED OF GOLD IN SCORING ROW.

text.p: Boxing controversy hit the Mediterranean Games on Monday when an Italian heavyweight was stripped of a gold medal in favour of an Algerian after a committee ruled that electronic scoring was faulty.
It was believed to be the first time that the high-tech computerised scoring method used at Olympics and world championships had been overruled.
The ruling came despite the earlier insistence of world amateur boxing body AIBA that the verdict was good.
Italian Giacobbe Fragomeni won the heavyweight gold on Thursday when he outpointed Algerian Mohammed Benguesmia, the team flag bearer, 3-2 on points.
The score took the crowd by surprise and Algeria made a formal complaint when it emerged that four of the five judges had Benguesmia ahead on their back-up scorecards.
The fifth judge scored it an 8-8 draw.

The International Committee of the Mediterranean Games declared after a hearing that Algeria's protest was upheld and Benguesmia should be awarded the gold due to a "flagrant malfunction of the computerised result".
Fragomeni was given the silver medal.

AIBA president Emil Jetchev, a Bulgarian, had been quoted earlier as saying that "the only valid verdict is the computerised one, 3-2 for the Italian". AIBA was not immediately available for comment after the decision.
Italian Olympic Committee (CONI) secretary general Raffaele Pagnozzi had said on Saturday that his country, which has dominated the Games, was willing to give the gold to Algeria.
"We are willing to hand back this gold medal," he told reporters. "We don't know what happened. Maybe the machines were wrongly set up or did not work properly."

Pagnozzi stuck to his position on Sunday, despite angry accusations by former Olympic gold medallist and Italian boxing team coach Patrizio Oliva that CONI's attitude had more to do with votes for Rome's 2004 Olympic bid.
Rome is one of five cities on the short-list for the Games and a front-runner to win when the International Olympic Committee decides in September.

Former Italian soccer federation chief Antonio Matarrese, chairman of the local Mediterranean Games organising committee, hinted as much on Sunday when he was quoted as saying: "There are superior interests involved."
"Who cares about Roma 2004," Oliva had said on Sunday.
"For years we have had similar verdicts against us and we put up with it in silence. I don't see how you can call Fragomeni's gold into question.

"There are no doubts. The fight finished in Fragomeni's favour. It doesn't matter if it was only one point. I'm not saying our man won easily, I just say that he won...What can we do? Change the rules for political reasons?"
Fragomeni said he would rather have had a re-match against the Algerian than "be robbed of the gold in such a way".
"This incident has made me the protagonist of the Mediterranean Games but I wish it had happened in another way," the Italian lamented.

The computerised scoring method, introduced at Olympic level in 1992 in Barcelona, involves five judges who sit around the ring scoring with coloured electronic buttons and has caused several controversies in amateur boxing.
Three of the five must strike a button within a second for a hit to be registered as a scoring blow.
At the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, anomalies frequently occurred with boxers being given standing counts by the ring referee despite no points being awarded to their opponents.
In Barcelona, the system caused a storm of protest when American light-flyweight world champion Eric Griffin lost to a Spaniard despite being way ahead on manual scoring.
